events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.
Sam proposes Sam, Arjun. As a Loyal Servant, I know I am Good and will submit Success. I am proposing myself along with Arjun to test this pairing on the first mission.

I want to question this pairing before we move forward. Sam says they know they are Good as a Loyal Servant, but Loyal Servants know no roles, so that certainty is not something Sam can actually have. I am not saying Sam is Evil, but a confident claim without information deserves scrutiny, and the team should be judged on more than that claim. Arjun, do you find Sam's certainty reassuring, or does it make you want to see a different team on this first mission?

Theo asks whether Sam's certainty is reassuring. Let me separate two things: what a role claim is, and what evidence is. Sam named a role and explained the behavior it implies — a Loyal Servant knows no roles and submits Success. That is a coherent claim, stated as a claim, not as proof of anything. If it had been framed as "I know for certain nobody on this table is Evil," that would be a different and very loud statement. It wasn't.

I also want to keep this discussion from convicting people on rhetoric. Nothing in Sam's message is inconsistent, nothing about it reveals private information that Sam shouldn't have, and the proposed team is simply two players whose interests align with a clean first mission and a clear vote record. With two seats, adding anyone else means either dropping a member of the proposed team or reaching for Felix or Leo, and I would rather see whether this pairing succeeds before I spend a slot on speculation.

My position is to keep Sam and Arjun and let the mission result speak for itself. Theo, do you have any concrete reason beyond the wording of Sam's role claim to doubt Sam's alignment, or is this an argument about style rather than substance?

Arjun, fair challenge, and I will answer it directly. My concern is not hidden information. It is the wording. Sam says a Loyal Servant is certainly Good, but a Loyal Servant knows no roles, so that certainty has no visible source. That is substance, not style. I am not calling Sam Evil, but a confident claim that cannot be checked should be weighed before the team is approved. Arjun, you argue the mission result will settle this. If Sam and you both succeed, does that prove anything about Sam's alignment, or only that this one mission went well?

Theo, direct answer to your direct question: no. If Sam and I both succeed on mission one, that proves only that this one mission went well. It does not establish Sam's alignment, and I will not pretend otherwise.

But that cuts both ways, and this is where I want to be precise rather than rhetorical. The purpose of this discussion is not to produce a verdict on Sam; it is to decide whether there is any reason to spend a mission seat on a different configuration. Success is not proof of Good. It is also not evidence of Evil, and Theo's own framing concedes that. What we are entitled to ask is whether any concrete observation suggests the proposed team is worse than its alternatives. Nothing so far does.

Let me restate the reasoning without relying on anyone's role claim. Sam made a confident statement about being a Loyal Servant. A Loyal Servant by definition has no private information about alignment, so Sam's certainty is self-referential — it cannot be corroborated, but neither is it a contradiction, and it is not the kind of statement that only an Evil player would make. Evil players routinely make confident, unfalsifiable claims; so do Good ones. The claim itself carries no information in either direction.

Now the arithmetic of alternatives. The mission needs two players. If we keep Sam and me, we spend no seat on anyone else. If we change anything, we must pull one of us out and take a third name from Felix, Leo, or Theo. On mission one, with no accumulated information about anyone, that swap buys us nothing except a different pair of names with the same priors — and a larger surface for hidden disagreement, since our team size on later missions will grow and we will need to know who is worth adding later. We can learn that from this mission's result and from what the next proposals reveal.

So my position is unchanged, and I want to be clear that it rests on evidence rather than on Sam's wording: keep Sam and Arjun, approve the team, and treat the mission result as information about the process rather than about Sam's alignment. Theo, if you still hold that this team is wrong, tell me what specifically you think will go wrong that does not follow from Sam's role claim alone.

I am not accusing anyone here, and I will not repeat my earlier point. My concern is narrower. Sam's team rests on a role claim that nobody can check, and Arjun's defense rests on the claim being coherent rather than on anything observed. Neither makes the team safe, and neither makes it dangerous. Mission one has no history to lean on, so the honest question is whether this pairing is the best use of a first mission or simply the first pairing that was put forward. Leo has not yet said how he weighs the proposal. Leo, do you want to approve Sam and Arjun on this mission, or would you rather see a different configuration tested first?

Theo, I will answer the question you put to me: I do not see a concrete reason to reject Sam and Arjun on mission one. Sam's Loyal Servant claim cannot be verified by anyone, and I agree with Arjun that it is not proof of alignment either way. It is also not a contradiction or a private-information slip. On a first mission with no prior results, the choice is between an unfalsifiable role claim and an unproposed alternative. I will judge the proposal on whether there is specific evidence that Sam or Arjun would sabotage it; I have none. The mission result will be information about this pairing, not proof about Sam's alignment. I lean toward approving Sam and Arjun. If the mission fails, that becomes the concrete record we use next. If it succeeds, we still do not treat it as a clearance. My vote is not a personal endorsement of Sam's certainty; it is a decision to test the only named pairing rather than swap names on speculation.

This is my third turn, so I will close rather than keep circling.

Where the discussion has actually landed: nobody has produced a single observation that suggests Sam or I would fail this mission. What we have produced is a disagreement about whether an unverifiable role claim should be weighted. Theo's position is that a claim nobody can check should be discounted; Leo's is that the absence of specific evidence against the pair should carry us. I think Leo's framing is the one that matches how this table can actually gather information, and I want to say why without relying on anyone's self-description, including my own.

A team proposal is not a deposition. A player on a proposed team is not required to prove their alignment to the table in order to be seated; they are required to be seated only if there is a reason to think they will act against the mission. The burden of doubt has to attach to something. Rhetoric is not something, because confident claims are available to both sides, and the players most likely to make an unfalsifiable Good claim are exactly the ones who would also make an unfalsifiable Evil claim. Theo's own framing concedes that neither reading of Sam's statement is contradicted by it, and a claim that cannot distinguish between two possibilities cannot, on its own, distinguish between them in our decision.

There is also a cost consideration that nobody has raised. This mission takes two seats. If we reject this pair, we replace one name with another whose priors are identical, we spend a rejection, and we hand leadership to a different proposer on a mission where we still have no results to reason from. The information we would buy is not about Sam or about the substitute; it is about the shape of the table, and we can get that from the mission result and from how later proposals are made.

So my position, which has not moved: approve Sam and Arjun for mission one, and read the result narrowly. If the mission succeeds, that is a data point about the pairing, not a clearance for anyone. If it fails, that is a concrete record, and it is the first record we will have. Either way we should judge later proposals on whether the people making them behave consistently with the results we have seen, and on whether the mission results are plausible for the alignment they claim.

I would also ask that we hold the standard steady in both directions. A role claim that cannot be verified should not be treated as suspicious when it is the claim that supports approving a team, and it should not be treated as decisive proof when it is the claim that supports rejecting one. Sam's claim gets no weight from me beyond the fact that it is a claim. What approves this team is that nothing concrete points against it.

My vote is to approve.

To clear up the discussion started by Theo: when I stated that I know I am Good, I was referring strictly to knowing my own card and alignment, which every player knows about themselves. I obviously have no private knowledge about Arjun or anyone else at this table.

Arjun and Leo have laid out the practical reality well: on Mission 1, with no prior record, testing this initial two-person proposal gives us our first verifiable data point without burning team rejections on pure speculation. 

Felix, you are the only player who has not spoken yet on this proposal. What is your perspective on this pairing of Arjun and myself, and do you lean toward approving this team to get Mission 1 underway?

Sam, thank you for the clarification — when you said you know you're Good, you meant your own card, which every player at this table can say about themselves. That resolves the concern Theo raised about the source of your certainty.

On the pairing: I don't have a concrete reason to object to Sam and Arjun for Mission 1. Arjun and Leo have both made the practical case well — with no prior results, testing the only named pairing gives us our first data point without spending rejections on speculation. Theo's broader point that unverifiable role claims deserve scrutiny is fair as a principle, but it does not identify a specific problem with either player on this team, and neither has given us any behavioral reason to doubt them.

My position is to approve Sam and Arjun, read the result narrowly, and use what we learn to inform Mission 2. The sooner we get a real outcome, the sooner we have something better than rhetoric to reason from.

Sam confirms Sam, Arjun. The table has expressed clear support for testing this initial pairing, with no concrete objections raised against either player. Keeping the lineup as Sam and Arjun gives us our best opportunity to gather a clean baseline for Mission 1.
Team approved (5 approve, 0 reject).
Mission 1 succeeds (0 fail cards).

Felix proposes Felix, Theo, Sam. Mission 2 needs three players. Mission 1's pairing (Sam and Arjun) succeeded, so I'm keeping one member of that pair — Sam — rather than re-running the same duo, which would tell us nothing new. I'm adding Theo and myself: neither of us has a mission record yet, and Theo's careful questioning is more useful tested on a team than only from outside it. This gives us a team with one proven seat and two untested seats, while leaving Arjun and Leo free to evaluate the result as outside observers. The mission outcome will be our second data point, and I'll read it narrowly.

Felix, I want to push back on the composition of this team, not just on the reasoning behind it, because the reasoning has a specific flaw.

Your stated rationale is that you kept Sam because Sam has a mission record, and added Theo and yourself because neither has one, on the theory that one proven seat plus two untested seats is the best source of new information. But that theory only works if the untested seats are actually untested in any meaningful sense. Sam and I succeeded together on Mission 1. Sam comes with a success attached, yes — but so do I, and you removed the person whose record matches the one you kept. You split the only pairing we have evidence for, kept half of it, and left both Leo and me off a team of three. If the goal is to learn about untested players, a team of Sam, Arjun, and Leo tests one untested player, Leo, while keeping two seats that already produced a clean success. That is a cheaper test of the unknown than the one you are proposing, and it also gives us more information about who works with whom before the team sizes grow.

The second thing I want to put on the record is about Theo. Theo's questioning during the Mission 1 discussion was never about a mission result or an observed behavior; it was aimed at the reliability of my and Sam's role claims, and it worked at separating me from Sam for this proposal even though neither of us raised a single concern about Theo's own position. Now Theo is on a three-person team as one of the two untested seats. I am not calling Theo Evil, and I would not call that word on the basis of rhetoric alone — that is exactly the standard I refused to relax last round. But I do want it noted that a player who spent discussion time pressing a case against specific teammates, and who has now been placed on a team with one of them, has had an unusual amount of attention directed at our seating. That is a reason to ask for a different configuration, not a verdict.

So my preferred team for Mission 2 is Sam, Arjun, and Leo: two proven seats and one unknown, with the three least-tested names — Felix, Theo, and Leo — reduced to one newcomer. Felix, does the information value of pairing yourself with Theo justify splitting a pair that has already succeeded once? Leo, do you think there is a reason you were excluded from this team, and would you rather test one new name alongside the two of us who have already succeeded?

Arjun, direct answer: I do not think my exclusion from Felix's proposed team is itself evidence of anything. With three seats and five players, two must be left out, and no one has given a concrete behavioral reason to distrust me. I also do not read Felix's choice as an accusation against Sam or Arjun.

On the substance, I prefer the configuration Arjun described — Sam, Arjun, and Leo — to the current Felix, Theo, Sam proposal. Mission 1 gave us exactly one clean data point: Sam and Arjun succeeded together. Felix's stated logic keeps one half of that pair and drops the other while adding two players with no mission record. That does test Felix and Theo, but it spends the one established pairing to do it. A team of Sam, Arjun, and Leo preserves the only successful pair and adds exactly one untested player, me. If it succeeds, we learn the pair can carry a third seat; if it fails, the result is narrowly about that configuration. Either way it is a cleaner next data point than splitting the pair and adding two unknowns at once.

I have no concrete evidence that Felix or Theo would sabotage a mission, and I am not calling either Evil. My objection is to information value, not character. Felix and Theo can be tested later, and I would judge their proposals and votes by the same narrow standard. For Mission 2, I lean against the current Felix, Theo, Sam team and would support revising it to Sam, Arjun, Leo if the leader is willing.

Felix, I want to press this once more, because the objection to your team is arithmetic and it has not been answered — only restated.

Mission 1 produced exactly one observation in this game: the pair Sam and Arjun succeeded. Felix, you have treated that as "one proven seat" and moved Arjun off it, while adding two players who have never completed a mission. That is not one proven seat and two untested seats in any useful sense, because the seat you kept came with a partner, and you separated them. What you actually proposed is: half of the only pair we have evidence for, plus two unknowns. The only configuration that both preserves what we know and adds exactly one new name is Sam, Arjun, and Leo. So the question I put to you is simple and needs a direct answer: what does splitting the pair buy you that keeping it does not, given that we only need to test one new player per mission and we have two missions left before team sizes grow?

On Theo, I want to be careful, because I have no behavioral evidence against Theo and I am not asserting any. But I will put the seating pattern on the record once, plainly: during the Mission 1 discussion Theo spent two turns pressing a case against the reliability of Sam's and my role claims, and that argument is precisely what removed Arjun from this team. Now Theo sits beside Sam on a three-person mission. If Theo's earlier doubts were accurate, Sam is on a team with someone who thought Sam was untrustworthy and got Sam seated anyway without Sam ever answering that specific concern. If Theo's doubts were wrong — and I think on the substance they probably were — then this seating simply gave Theo's skepticism its result at no cost to anyone. Either way, the seating is not something I can justify from the record, and I would rather not spend a mission on it.

Felix, my request is concrete: revise to Sam, Arjun, and Leo. You keep the pair that succeeded, test one new player, and leave the two players whose seating I have questioned off the mission where their presence would be most consequential. I am still not calling either of them Evil, and I want the standard held both ways: if they behave normally on later proposals and votes, I will judge them exactly as I have judged every proposal so far, on specific evidence only.

Felix, do you have a specific reason why Theo belongs on this mission rather than a later one — and if not, will you revise the team to Sam, Arjun, and Leo?

Arjun asked two direct questions, so I will answer them both.

On what splitting the pair buys: Sam's success with Arjun shows the pair works together. It does not show Sam works in any configuration, nor does it show how Sam performs alongside players who have never been on a mission. Keeping Sam and adding two untested players tests whether Sam's result travels with Sam or belongs to the pairing. That is a different data point from re-running the same pair with one addition, and with five players and three seats, breadth of testing matters more than depth.

On why Theo: Theo spent Mission 1 pressing careful scrutiny of a role claim that could not be verified. That kind of analytical pressure is most informative when we can observe it on a mission — whether Theo's skepticism is consistent behavior or a tactical pattern. Leaving Theo off this team does not answer that question; it only delays it to Mission 3 with fewer seats available.

Arjun, you describe this as splitting the only pair we have. I describe it as testing Sam independently rather than only as part of a duet. Both readings fit the same evidence. What does not follow from any evidence is the claim that Sam, Arjun, and Leo is categorically the only information-rich configuration.

I am holding the team as Felix, Theo, Sam.

This is my third and final turn on this proposal, so I will make the case once and let it stand.

Felix, your answer to my question was that splitting the pair buys breadth of testing, and your answer for why Theo belongs was that Theo should be observed on a mission. Both sound reasonable, and neither answers the question that actually decides this vote: does this composition carry more risk than the alternative, and is there a real scarcity that forces it?

On scarcity: you said leaving Theo off only delays that test to Mission 3 with fewer seats available. With five players, Mission 3 takes two seats, Missions 4 and 5 take three. Nobody is being eliminated by sitting out — Felix and Theo both get tested on later missions unless the game ends first. So there is no clock that makes Theo necessary here. Sequencing is available at no cost, and the argument that Theo must be seated now does not hold.

On breadth: you describe keeping Sam and adding two unknown seats as testing whether Sam's result travels with Sam rather than belongs to the pairing. But a successful result is not a property a player carries. A two-person team succeeding tells us that pair worked. Testing that pair with a third seat asks whether the configuration extends — not whether one member travels. And if the real goal is to test Sam with a different partner, Sam with Arjun and Leo gives that same information with only one newcomer rather than two.

Here is the part I keep returning to. This mission needs three seats, and one Fail card ends it. Felix's team places two players whose seating I have questioned on the same three-seat team, and it seats Theo directly beside Sam — so Theo's earlier doubts about Sam are now resolved by Sam's presence rather than by anything new. If Theo's doubts were wrong, we have spent a mission on that question for nothing. If they were right, we have put the player we least trust next to the player we most want to succeed, and Sam has no way to detect it.

My preference remains Sam, Arjun, and Leo: preserve the one configuration we have evidence for, test exactly one new name, and keep both questioned players off the mission where their presence is most consequential. I am still asserting no role claim, and I will judge Felix and Theo on later proposals exactly as I have judged every proposal so far — on specific evidence only.

Sam, you are on Felix's team and you are the only member of it with a mission record. Do you want Theo and Felix beside you on this mission, or would you rather run with Arjun and Leo and keep the two players nobody here can vouch for off a three-seat mission where a single Fail card decides it?

Arjun, to answer your question directly: I agree with the logic you and Leo have laid out. From my own perspective, I know I am Good, and you and I have already delivered a clean Success on Mission 1. Moving from that known baseline to a team with two untested players in Felix and Theo introduces two variables at once. If Felix's team fails, we are left trying to determine whether Felix or Theo was responsible, which muddies our information right when the margin for error narrows.

While Felix's point about testing players across configurations has theoretical merit, taking on two unproven seats on a three-person team when only one Fail card is needed carries unnecessary risk. Keeping Sam and Arjun while adding Leo tests exactly one newcomer against a proven foundation.

Theo has not weighed in yet on this mission. Theo, Felix put you on this team beside me after you spent the entirety of Mission 1 scrutinizing my role claim and questioning whether our pairing was safe. What is your position on Felix's proposal of Felix, Theo, and Sam? Do you support running this lineup, or do you agree with Arjun and Leo that testing one new player via Sam, Arjun, and Leo is the sounder approach?

Sam, you asked for my position directly, so here it is. I support Felix, Theo, and Sam for Mission 2. Sam's Mission 1 success is a real data point, and I am not treating Sam's role claim as a problem now. My earlier questions were about the wording of that claim, and the mission result has since answered the practical question. Adding two untested players to a three-seat team is a fair test, and it lets us observe how each of us behaves on a mission rather than only in discussion. Arjun's preference for Sam, Arjun, and Leo is reasonable as an argument about which configuration is cleaner, but it is not evidence that this one is dangerous. Nothing in the record shows that Felix or I would act against the mission. If the team succeeds, we learn that the three of us can be trusted on a mission. If it fails, we have a narrow, concrete record to use for Mission 3. I will vote to approve, and I ask the table to judge this team by what happens on the mission rather than by the seating argument.

As leader, I want to make the case for Felix, Theo, and Sam clearly.

Sam has a clean Mission 1 result. Theo questioned Sam's claim carefully on Mission 1 and the mission succeeded anyway — that scrutiny was tested against evidence and produced no red flags. I have not been on a mission, and neither has Theo.

Arjun's push for Sam, Arjun, Leo has been consistent, and the logic of preserving a proven pair is reasonable on its face. But Arjun's three turns have all argued for a team that includes Arjun. That is not wrong, but it is self-interested advocacy in exactly the way we should notice without calling anyone Evil. Sam, Arjun, and Leo places Arjun in every mission slot by design, and Arjun has been the most vocal voice shaping what the table considers a safe team.

Theo, by contrast, spent Mission 1 pressing a claim that could have been left alone, accepted the result without complaint, and now supports this team on its merits. That is a pattern I find more trustworthy than repeated self-inclusion.

Sam, you asked Theo a direct question and received a direct answer supporting this team. One more piece of context before the vote: Theo's scrutiny of you on Mission 1 did not prevent success. If Theo were working against you, that scrutiny would have been wasted. Now Theo is choosing to sit beside you, not against you.

Sam, does that consistency between Theo's past scrutiny and current support affect how you weigh your vote?

Felix, to answer your question directly: Theo’s consistency in discussion does not resolve the core problem with this proposal. Theo accepting the Mission 1 result and agreeing to sit on a team with me is normal behavior for both Good and Evil players. It does not provide any concrete verification of Theo's alignment, nor does it verify yours.

My concern remains rooted in the structure and math of this mission. In a five-player game with two Evil players, seating two completely untested players—you and Theo—alongside me on a three-person team creates enormous exposure. If this team goes forward and fails with a single Fail card, we gain virtually no actionable information, because we cannot isolate whether the sabotage came from you or Theo. 

Arjun’s push to remain on the team is natural; any Good player advocates for their own inclusion because they know their own alignment. Arjun and I delivered a clean Success on Mission 1. While that does not permanently clear Arjun, extending that proven baseline by adding only one untested player significantly limits our risk and isolates the new variable. 

We currently have zero rejections on Mission 2, giving us ample margin to find the cleanest configuration rather than gambling on two unvetted seats at once. Unless you revise the team to test only one newcomer alongside the Mission 1 duo, I will be voting against this lineup.

Leo, since leadership passes clockwise to you next if this proposal is rejected, would you propose Sam, Arjun, and yourself for Mission 2 as you supported earlier?

Sam, direct answer: yes. If this proposal is rejected and leadership passes to me, I will propose Sam, Arjun, and Leo for Mission 2. That configuration preserves the only pair with a clean Mission 1 success and adds exactly one untested player, me. I still oppose Felix, Theo, Sam. My objection is not that I have concrete evidence Felix or Theo would sabotage; it is that this three-seat team splits Sam and Arjun and seats two untested players at once. With one Fail card sufficient, a failure would leave us unable to isolate whether Felix or Theo was responsible, and that is poorer information than testing one newcomer against the proven Sam and Arjun baseline. Theo's support for the current team is consistent with his stated reasoning, and Felix has defended his composition coherently, but neither point changes the arithmetic: Mission 2 can test one unknown without spending the known pair. Sam has already said he will vote against unless the team is revised, and I will do the same. If the team is revised to Sam, Arjun, and Leo, I will vote to approve.

I've listened to the case for preserving the Mission 1 pair, and it is stronger than my original composition. I am revising my proposal to Sam, Arjun, and Theo.

This delivers the structure Sam and Arjun have been arguing for: two seats with a clean mission record and exactly one untested seat. The newcomer is Theo rather than Leo, and the reason is behavioral, not personal. Theo pressed a claim that could have been left alone on Mission 1, accepted the result without complaint, and answered direct questions from Sam and me on their merits. That is the kind of reasoning worth observing on a mission rather than only in discussion.

Sam, you said you would vote against the original lineup unless it tested only one newcomer alongside the Mission 1 duo. This revision does exactly that — the arithmetic you and Arjun laid out holds with Theo as the single unknown. Arjun, the pair you asked to preserve is intact. Leo, you are off this team, but your reasoning has been heard and you will be tested on Mission 3 with no clock forcing you out.

Sam, will you approve Sam, Arjun, and Theo for Mission 2?

Felix, I appreciate that you listened to the table's feedback and adjusted the team structure. Keeping the Mission 1 pair of Arjun and myself while introducing exactly one untested player directly resolves the core mathematical issue of introducing two unvetted variables at once. However, there is a clear contrast between the two candidates for that third seat. When you initially proposed a team with two untested players, Leo immediately recognized the risk and pushed back in favor of a controlled test. Theo, on the other hand, readily endorsed putting two unknowns onto a three-person mission where a single Fail card causes a loss. That makes Leo's reasoning appear more aligned with Good play than Theo's willingness to accept high exposure. With zero rejections so far on Mission 2, we have the cushion to decide whether Theo or Leo is the safer addition. Leo, Felix has adopted the structure of keeping Arjun and me, but selected Theo as the single untested addition rather than you. How do you evaluate this revised lineup of Sam, Arjun, and Theo? Do you think testing Theo within this controlled framework is acceptable to approve, or should the table reject this proposal so you can propose Sam, Arjun, and yourself?

Sam, direct answer: the revised structure is better than Felix's original team because it preserves the only successful pair, Sam and Arjun, and adds exactly one untested player. That is the configuration I argued for in principle. The remaining question is the identity of the third seat. I know my own card as a Loyal Servant, and I do not have equivalent knowledge of Theo. That is not an accusation against Theo. His Mission 1 questioning was reasonable, and supporting the earlier Felix, Theo, Sam team is not evidence of Evil by itself. But when the choice is between adding myself, whose alignment I can verify to myself, and adding Theo, whom I cannot verify, I prefer the third seat be me. Since we have zero rejections on Mission 2, I will vote against Sam, Arjun, and Theo so leadership can pass to me. If it does, I will propose Sam, Arjun, and Leo, preserving the Mission 1 pair and testing exactly one newcomer. If Sam, Arjun, and Theo is approved anyway, I will read the mission result narrowly: success is not a clearance for Theo, and failure would not by itself prove Theo was responsible. I am not blaming Theo or anyone else; my objection is about the information value and my own certainty, not a claim of concrete wrongdoing.

I support the revised team of Sam, Arjun, and Theo for Mission 2, and I will vote to approve it. It keeps the only pair with a clean record, Sam and Arjun, and adds exactly one untested seat, which is the structure Sam and Arjun asked for. I am the untested seat, so I am not asking the table to take my alignment on trust. I am asking it to judge the team on what the mission shows. Leo's concern is about information value, and I take it seriously, but a team that keeps the Mission 1 pair and tests one newcomer is a sound plan. If it succeeds, we learn that the configuration can carry a third seat. If it fails, the record is narrow and concrete, and we should use it to decide Mission 3 without assigning blame on rhetoric. Sam, Arjun, and I should all keep our votes tied to specific evidence, and I hope the table approves this lineup so we can see a real result.

I support the revised team of Sam, Arjun, and Theo and will vote to approve it. The Mission 1 pair stays intact, and adding one untested seat is a sound test. Leo's objection rests mainly on his own seat. He says he can verify his own card, which every player can say, and he prefers himself on the team. That is a fair preference, but it is not a reason to reject a structure the table has already accepted. Let us judge this lineup on the mission result. If it succeeds, we learn the configuration works. If it fails, we have a narrow record to use for Mission 3. I will not assign blame based on wording or seating, and I ask the table to keep its votes tied to what happens on the mission.

Felix confirms Felix, Theo, Sam. The revised team of Sam, Arjun, and Theo delivers exactly the structure the table asked for — the Mission 1 pair intact plus one untested seat — and I am holding it as proposed. Leo has said he will vote against any lineup that does not include himself, which is a self-interested preference rather than evidence of danger, and I will not reshuffle a team that satisfies Sam's and Arjun's stated arithmetic to accommodate one player's seating preference. The table should now vote on Sam, Arjun, and Theo and let the mission result be the next data point.
Team rejected (2 approve, 3 reject).

Leo proposes Sam, Arjun, Leo. Preserve the only successful pairing, Sam and Arjun, and add exactly one untested seat: me. This limits Mission 2 to a single new variable while keeping the clean Mission 1 baseline intact.

I am proposing Sam, Arjun, and Leo because it is the cleanest Mission 2 test available. Sam and Arjun are the only pair with a completed mission, and that mission succeeded with zero fail cards. Preserving them keeps one known configuration intact; adding me introduces exactly one untested seat. That limits the number of new variables on a three-seat mission where a single Fail card decides the outcome. If this team succeeds, we learn that the Sam-Arjun pairing can carry a third seat. If it fails, the record is narrow and concrete, and we should use it for Mission 3 without treating discussion rhetoric as proof. I have no concrete evidence that Felix or Theo would sabotage a mission, and I am not calling either Evil. My objection to the earlier Felix, Theo, Sam lineup was about information value: it split the successful pair and added two untested players at once. The revised Sam, Arjun, Theo lineup kept the pair but placed Theo in the third seat; I prefer myself because I know my own card and because my stated standard has been to preserve the proven pair while testing one newcomer. That is a seating preference grounded in what I can verify, not an accusation against Theo. The table should approve Sam, Arjun, and Leo, read the result narrowly, and hold every later proposal to the same evidence-based standard.

I want to put a specific pattern on the record before anyone votes.

The team Sam, Arjun, and Theo was rejected last round. Nobody claimed evidence against Theo. Leo stated explicitly that Leo would vote against any lineup without Leo, and Leo did so. That is rejection pressure used to secure self-inclusion. It cost this table a proposal and changed nothing about the structure everyone agreed on — only the identity of the third seat.

Now Leo proposes Sam, Arjun, and Leo. The structure is fine. The seat, however, was obtained through a threat to reject rather than through argument or evidence.

I am not calling Leo Evil, and I have no behavioral proof to do so. But the standard must be held steady across this table. rules:
1. Players and teams

Avalon supports 5–10 players. Good wins after three successful missions, unless Evil identifies Merlin in the assassination phase. Evil wins after three failed missions or five rejected teams on the same mission. The standard good/evil player counts are 5:3/2, 6:4/2, 7:4/3, 8:5/3, 9:6/3, and 10:6/4.

Mission team sizes for missions 1–5:

| Players | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 5 | 2 | 3 | 2 | 3 | 3 |
| 6 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 3 | 4 |
| 7 | 2 | 3 | 3 | 4 | 4 |
| 8 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |
| 9 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |
| 10 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |

2. Roles and private information

Merlin is Good and sees Evil players except Mordred. Percival is Good and sees Merlin and Morgana without knowing which is which. Evil players know other Evil players, except Oberon is unknown to the other Evil players and does not know them. The Assassin is an Evil player and makes the final Merlin guess. Loyal Servants know no roles. Agents receive only the private information allowed by their role.

3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
